title: Transform Data Using Notebooks (Microsoft Fabric Tutorial Series)
summary: A practitioner walkthrough of Fabric notebooks for data transformation, covering runtime specifics, capacity/cold-start behavior, production patterns (schema enforcement, idempotent merges, incremental ingestion), and a decision guide for when to pick notebooks over Dataflow Gen2 or the SQL warehouse.
audience: Data engineers already comfortable with PySpark who are ramping up on Fabric-specific notebook mechanics and orchestration.
why_it_matters: Goes beyond generic Spark/PySpark instruction into Fabric-specific operational details — capacity SKU cold-start timing, mssparkutils parameterization, V-Order/Liquid Clustering defaults, and concrete cost/latency tradeoffs against Dataflow Gen2 and the SQL warehouse — that are easy to get wrong when moving from open-source Spark habits to Fabric.
takeaways: Notebook cold-start time depends on capacity SKU size, not just being 'cold' vs 'warm'.
An attached Lakehouse changes how unqualified table names resolve, which is a common source of confusion when switching lakehouses mid-project.
Fabric's default engine behaviors (V-Order on, default shuffle partition count) are tuning levers practitioners should know rather than leave unexamined.
Notebooks, Dataflow Gen2, and the SQL warehouse are not interchangeable — the source frames a scenario-by-scenario decision matrix rather than a single 'best' tool.
Time-travel and VACUUM retention interact: shortening retention silently breaks downstream point-in-time queries.

claims.text: Per the post, Fabric notebook cold start takes roughly 20 to 60 seconds on F2-F4 capacities but drops to under 20 seconds on F8 and larger SKUs.
An attached Lakehouse is required before a notebook can write Delta tables, and unqualified table names in code resolve against whichever Lakehouse is currently attached.
Switching the attached Lakehouse partway through a project forces a rewrite of any unqualified table references in the notebook's code, since they no longer resolve to the same tables.

Per the post, incremental ingestion in Fabric notebooks is commonly parameterized using mssparkutils.runtime.getParameterValue so a pipeline can pass in a run date and the notebook reads only that day's partition.
Fabric notebooks have no native scheduling of their own; recurring execution is handled exclusively by wrapping the notebook in a Data Factory pipeline notebook activity.
V-Order is described as enabled by default on Fabric Delta tables and is recommended to leave on rather than disable.

Reducing Delta VACUUM retention below the default about 7-day window is flagged as risky because it can cause downstream time-travel queries against older snapshots to fail once those versions are purged.

The post frames the notebook-versus-Dataflow-Gen2 choice around scale and audience: notebooks suit large recurring transforms (its example is a daily 10GB-plus load) while Dataflow Gen2 suits low-code, business-user-driven visual mapping.

The post notes Fabric notebook library installs via %pip install apply only to the current interactive session, and recommends workspace-level library management instead for libraries that must persist across notebook runs.
